title: City development in Trondheim
sentences: But when you're at a dinner then and you notice the engagement, what is it people care about?
Well a lot of people care about Olav Tryggvason's street when they meet me at least,
and then a lot of people care about things like the Nidarø hall, yes, car access, parking
The square maybe?
The square yes, but maybe not as much as you might have expected,
but that was perhaps a bit earlier when it was much more unclear.
Now you know more about progress and what's going to happen, yes,
but a lot about that accessibility thing and opening and closing bridges and yes.
Is it mostly negative or is there something positive?
I'd say all engagement is positive and I'm a very engaged person so I think it's really fun to discuss city development,
but in some forums you get a bit of a stamp,
or you get stamped as,
We're a bunch of idiots I've been told a few times and that can be a bit like,
how do you take that then,
I mean we are highly educated people and it is
We really do have a good overview of city development here in Trondheim but also in other Norwegian cities and foreign cities,
but nobody has the answer,
because if someone had the brilliant answer to how we should have built the city
or how we should develop the centre we would have done it, and that's exactly it, that it's so complex,
That we need all those different voices and need to discuss,
and I can happily go into a shop in the city centre and start discussing centre development
because I want to hear those different voices,
because there are many good inputs from different people I think, different actors, that nobody has the whole truth or the whole answer.
No, and maybe there isn't a right answer either?
No there isn't, because who has built the perfect city?
I haven't seen it anyway.
And a certain matter-of-factness in the debate is what you want then.
Yes I'm really for fact-based city development, so one of the things I've helped introduce since I started at Trondheim municipality is the Midtbyen accounts,
I don't know if you've heard of it,
but it's exactly about getting facts on the table that we can agree on,
both business and the municipality and yes both the retailers and property owners and.
We can have something we say we agree on and that's fact,
and then we should agree on the goals, and then we can discuss the measures,
instead of disagreeing about the goal and where we are today and where we're going and the measures, then it all gets mixed up.
But we're talking now about, and stating that there's a lot of engagement around city development,
and then the question becomes how can this engagement be used in the work on plans and strategies?
Well I think we in the municipality have a particular need
and wish to get input from different actors in Trondheim.
First of all we have a very highly educated and competent population,
I mean we have 200,000 clever heads in this city who can help us.
On top of that we have a very enterprising business community that knows where the shoe pinches,
and we have a lot of voluntary organisations, and we have other public agencies, I mean we're very lucky in Trondheim I think.
My god how lucky we are, we just have to make good use of these resources,
and then you have to use different arenas and different tools to get those different voices involved.
Because there's always someone who goes very quiet in a gathering where you feel that someone is more important than you,
or who in a way has more to contribute,
so it's about establishing different kinds of participation and input arenas.
I know you've been working on that lately, developing the arenas where people can take part,
can you give some examples of what you've done or are going to do on that front?
Yes, we at the city planning office have worked a lot on participation,
and that's because it's something of the moment.
I think a kind of paradigm shift is happening right now, that you're supposed to create the city together,
but this past year in connection with us having,
We've made, or we're making, both a centre strategy and a city development strategy and plans for local centres in Trondheim,
so we've joined forces and tried out some new tools and new arenas,
and we've had for example city-development dinner parties and we've had a citizens' panel on city development.
We have a lot of workshops where we map existing values on a map today.
We try to build Lego to see how the city should look in the future.
We use a lot of digital tools and now we're using a 3D model to see and make city development more understandable both for residents and for politicians,
I think that's really important,
to make it more understandable, to raise awareness before you make choices.
So you're trying out different things?
Yes I'd say lately we've been testing things and we've got a lot, we've got grant money for that too.
